newsitem.title: CANADA: The long war (or bore) is over.
newsitem.headline: The long war (or bore) is over.

text.p: We're facing 25 years of freedom from browser wars, much less chance of dying of boredom and a safer Internet environment for the whole world.
You got a problem with that?

You may have noticed recently that the fearsome "browser wars" were about to heat up again because that Redmond company run by that rich young newlywed is about to release the latest "test" version of the Internet Explorer browser.

The new browser, which in fact is not really all that new, is dubbed "Preview 2, 4.0", and is free to download should you not mind dropping another anvil of software code on to your already bursting hard drive.

But perhaps you recoiled in horror, sitting on your deck chair, and the ice cubes in your glass tinkled while your hand trembled, as you recalled the last browser wars and the havoc it wreaked on your mental well being.
Last year it was hardly safe to venture outside without being bombarded with the latest salvo in the war between the Microsoft Corp. and Netscape Communications Corp.
"How to Know Who'll Win the Browser Wars" and "The War Rages On" were only some of the headlines that froze us in our chairs, unsettled the children and skittered the cat.
But here's the new formula for success in cyberspace: hype is bad. Staying calm is good.

If people stay calm and apply this to their everyday lives and only get really excited when a major work of art is made or when a new Douglas Coupland novel comes out in paperback, then the entire global community can, well, stay calm.
But if the world takes the hype route, that starts a vicious cycle that pulls everyone toward boredom.

If people get excited when a browser adds some new widget such as "integration options" or "channels" of even lesser consequence that what's already offered on cable, then people will turn in on themselves, which leads to rigidity of thought, boring parties and lousy content everywhere.

But if we take the non-hype route, people will not be fooled into testing every small change in a piece of software or buying the first package that promises to let you endlessly "patch" the product with software "updates" over the Net.
It will be like going to a bakery and refusing to buy the half-baked cookies and instead waiting for a finished, tasty batch.
Finally, being free of overblown hype is not based on a set of hopeful predictions but a course of events that could well help us all.

First off, children will be taught early in school never to use the word "salvo." This should ensure that any future headline writers in the primary grades will never attempt construction such as "Such and such company fires another salvo in browser war."
They will be told to repeat salvo five times each morning, which would cure anybody of using such a strange word.

Next, universities will teach what is really important in life. Such as that when one turns on the water what really matters is not the look of the tap fixture or how many knobs it has but the quality of the water.
So with people so educated, software companies will be forced to deliver enriching, intelligent and even fun content on the Web and millions of people will thank them big time.
